title: Build and review a business plan: evidence before commitment
summary: Follow the customer, offer, delivery, economics, funding and responsibility decisions that make a plan useful.
takeaway: A plan should expose assumptions and guide the next decision; a checklist cannot predict success at a glance.

visuals.title: Six connected business-plan decisions
visuals.note: Return to an earlier decision when new evidence changes its assumptions.

ranges.heading: A plan is a decision document

paragraphs: The opening claim that a glance can reveal business success or failure is unsupported. Use an executive summary to state the decision, evidence and unresolved assumptions; a company description should identify the business, history, mission, industry, operations, people and financial position. A persuasive document is not proof of viability.

ranges.heading: Supporting evidence and legal review
ranges.introduction: The legal-counsel heading is undeveloped in the supplied notes. Retain it as a review requirement rather than inventing a jurisdiction-specific legal checklist. Select the supporting material that helps the reader assess the actual decision.

paragraphs: The legal-entity list mixes jurisdiction-specific forms and categories; LLP, LLC, private limited and society are not interchangeable in every country. Flat, step, net, cost-of-living and percentage leases describe payment/cost structures, not a complete property-law checklist. An SLA needs scope, service measures and remedies. Preserve these prompts while obtaining the applicable professional review.

editorialSections.heading: 1. Establish the customer and problem
paragraphs: Record who experiences the problem, how urgent it is, which alternatives they use and what evidence could change your view. Follow the venture-validation and market-segmentation guides.

editorialSections.heading: 2. Test the offer and model
paragraphs: State the value proposition and business-model assumptions. Choose a PoC, prototype or MVP to answer a defined question, then record what you learned rather than declaring fit from a launch.

links.label: Choose a PoC, prototype or MVP

editorialSections.heading: 3. Plan delivery and people
paragraphs: Connect capabilities, suppliers, facilities, workflow, roles and decision rights. Use the organization, operations and project guides for the detailed methods; identify the constraints and owners.

links.label: Define a project when one is needed

editorialSections.heading: 4. Review economics and uncertainty
paragraphs: Separate recorded facts, assumptions, forecasts and judgments. Assess cash, working capital, break-even and scenarios with defined periods and units; use the existing finance references.

editorialSections.heading: 5. Choose funding and explain the case
paragraphs: Match the funding need to its timing, repayment capacity and control implications. Compare routes before negotiating terms; keep the investor story consistent with the evidence and use of proceeds.

editorialSections.heading: 6. Assign responsibility and revisit
paragraphs: Identify affected stakeholders, risks, ethical obligations and escalation routes. Review the plan when evidence or conditions change, with clear owners and next decisions.

title: Validate a venture: from problem evidence to market learning
summary: Organize customer questions, learning activities and measures around the uncertainty they address.
takeaway: Interest, clicks and a prototype are evidence inputs; none alone proves product–market fit.

visuals.title: Match uncertainty to evidence
rows: That your proposed solution will be purchased
That a feasible product can deliver value
Task success, technical performance and repeated use
Sustainable unit economics or market fit
Retention, payment, referrals and defined cohorts
A permanent fit across every segment
visuals.note: Editorial comparison; all supplied questions and activity names remain in the detailed sections.

ranges.heading: Four working labels, not a guaranteed ladder

paragraphs: The source distinguishes problem exploration, problem–solution fit, “solution–product fit” and product–market fit. The third label is source terminology, not presented as a universal standard. Teams may revisit stages; define the evidence needed for the actual customer and business model.

ranges.heading: Questions to investigate
ranges.introduction: Keep the four sets of questions connected to their intended uncertainty: customer/problem, response to a solution, product feasibility/value, and actual use/payment/referral.

ranges.heading: Artifacts and experiments
ranges.introduction: Choose the least costly artifact that answers the question. The source places an MVP beside early solution tests and analysis beside later build activities; treat this as a menu rather than mandatory project sequencing.

ranges.heading: Measurements and their limits
ranges.introduction: Preserve qualitative feedback alongside behavioural and commercial measures. NPS is a recommendation measure, not a complete satisfaction score; LTV and a viral coefficient require explicit definitions. Interest metrics do not by themselves demonstrate retention or willingness to pay.

title: PoC, prototype or MVP: choose the uncertainty to reduce
summary: Compare technical experiments, representations of an experience and a minimum viable market-learning offer.
takeaway: Choose by the question and evidence required, not by a fixed number of weeks or an assumed price tag.

visuals.title: Choose a learning vehicle
rows: Can a critical technical mechanism work?
Can people understand/use the proposed experience?
Will a real offer create enough value to support the next decision?
Isolate and test a technical assumption
Represent a flow, interaction or concept
Deliver a deliberately limited offer and observe use
Experience, clarity and fit to a task
Scope dependent; source suggests days/weeks and a small budget
Scope dependent; source suggests weeks and a medium budget
Scope dependent; source suggests months and a defined budget
Technical results and possible user input
Behavioural and qualitative evidence from real use
Not required to grow customers or earn revenue
Not required to grow customers or earn revenue
Possible outcomes; neither is guaranteed or always necessary for the test
Refine feasibility or proceed to a prototype/MVP
Revise the experience or test a viable offer
Iterate, expand, change direction or stop
visuals.note: This replaces the categorical teaching claims with conditional comparisons; every original row remains accessible in the source disclosure.

ranges.heading: A contextual comparison, not fixed definitions

paragraphs: The source table includes goal, time, audience, use, risk, budget, feedback, growth, revenue and next steps. Its durations and funding/revenue claims describe possible examples, not required properties. A PoC can receive user feedback; a prototype need not raise investment; an MVP need not take months or immediately earn revenue.

Technical feasibility, usability and market demand can overlap, but they are different questions. An MVP does not guarantee product–market fit. Preserve the original comparison below while using the clarified table for decisions.

title: Pitch a venture: connect the story to evidence
summary: Build a concise account of the customer problem, business model, viability and investment decision.
takeaway: The narrative should make the evidence understandable; it cannot replace validation or disclosure of risks.

paragraphs: A 30-second version can clarify an opening pitch; it is not a universal required format. Exposition, complication, climax, reversal and resolution offer a storytelling structure. The “95% story / 5% deal” split and the bystander-to-visionary hierarchy have no supporting evidence in the supplied notes. Treat them as prompts, not investor-behaviour statistics.

ranges.heading: The value case behind the story
ranges.introduction: Show the proposition, strategic vision, business-case validation, operating viability, assumptions, risks and competitive position. Explain segment, value chain/network, costs and profit without pretending a compelling vision verifies the numbers.

title: Funding readiness: the need, evidence and investor fit
summary: Review why funding is needed, what has been demonstrated and how a proposed investor fits the business.
takeaway: Capital has timing, risk and control implications; investor fit is more specific than a wish for high returns.

ranges.heading: Investor fit and the cost of raising too early

paragraphs: Raising can divert attention from customer evidence and delivery, add obligations and create unsuitable terms. The source’s portfolio/income statements describe mixed investor preferences, not universal requirements. Its S$50k/S$25k versus S$100k/S$250k example gives no clear denominator, period or risk basis; no performance ratio is inferred.

ranges.heading: Funding is an outcome of a case
ranges.introduction: The short “effective ways to get fund” label introduces a list, not a validated recipe.

ranges.heading: Readiness evidence to assemble
ranges.introduction: Discuss financial performance, growth, cash flow, recurring revenue, the value proposition, customers and management. “Overdepence” is preserved as a likely overdependence prompt; identify the specific concentration risk rather than inventing its meaning.

title: Founder investment terms: economics, control and exit
summary: Distinguish preference rights, information, board authority, founder incentives and transaction restrictions.
takeaway: A familiar term can operate very differently under a different agreement; read the economic and control effects together.
notes: Model-document references illustrate jurisdiction-specific provisions, not universally applicable contract terms.

references.title: SVCA / Singapore Academy of Law: VIMA model agreements
NVCA: US model legal documents

visuals.title: Separate four negotiations
rows: Who receives what under each outcome?
Voting, board seats, approval and information rights
Who can decide, veto or inspect?
What happens on departure, sale or another defined event?
Who is bound, for how long, and under what conditions?
visuals.note: Illustrative questions; enforceability and precise rights depend on the signed documents and jurisdiction.

ranges.heading: Terms to examine in a proposed investment
ranges.introduction: The notes mix economic rights, governance approvals, fees, vesting, proceeds, board composition and forbearance. They are a negotiation review menu, not standardized contractual language.

paragraphs: Double-trigger acceleration typically requires two specified events; the agreement defines them and the effect. Co-sale and no-shop clauses need scope, participants, duration and exceptions. The source’s “mutually don’t find new party” is not a universal definition of no-shop. These are deal terms, not automatic fundraising tactics.

title: Business financing routes: match the source to the need
summary: Separate lenders and investors from financing instruments, repayment patterns and trading venues.
takeaway: Compare cost, timing, security, cash-flow obligations and control before comparing labels.

visuals.title: Compare routes by obligation
rows: Available cash, concentration and personal exposure
Repayment, security, covenants, recourse and timing
Ownership dilution, governance, risk appetite and exit expectations
Eligibility, permitted use, reporting and repayment conditions
Supplier terms, factoring recourse, leases and working-capital effects
visuals.note: No route is recommended without the business’s specific cash needs and agreement terms.

ranges.heading: Loans, trade instruments and repayment features
ranges.introduction: This list combines financing purposes, collateral, repayment types, guarantees and credit instruments. A letter of credit is not simply an ordinary cash loan; Lombard lending generally refers to lending against pledged financial assets. Terms, availability and recourse need the actual contract.

paragraphs: Self-financing, angels, venture capital, crowdlending and grants describe different funding routes. PIPE means private investment in public equity; an OTC market is a trading venue, not an interchangeable startup investor. Hedge funds, acquisitions, swaps, barter and an ESOP are not all ordinary sources of venture equity. Trade credit, factoring and credit facilities belong with working-capital obligations. Asset and share deals differ in what is acquired and which obligations remain; legal/tax consequences depend on the transaction.

title: Business analysis: turn questions into supported recommendations
summary: Connect fact quality, assumptions and the BADIR workflow to a decision people can act on.
takeaway: A recommendation should trace back to a question, suitable evidence and an assessment of alternative explanations.

visuals.title: From uncertainty to action
rows: Recommend an action with evidence and limits
visuals.note: Exploration generates hypotheses; confirmatory analysis needs safeguards against choosing a test after seeing the answer.

ranges.heading: Facts, forecasts and judgment
ranges.introduction: The supplied hierarchy is a prompt to distinguish existing observations, accessible numbers, non-numeric facts, forecasts, expertise and assumptions. It is not a rule that an easy-to-find number is more reliable than a carefully designed study. Make assumptions explicit, benchmark them and test sensitivities.

ranges.heading: BADIR: a workflow for a business question
ranges.introduction: Keep Business question, Analysis plan, Data collection, Insights and Recommendations connected. Specify population, period, granularity, validation and alternative explanations. An 80/20 cut or “shunting long tail” may discard important cases; document that choice and test its effect.

title: Organization design: parts, coordination and decision rights
summary: Compare Mintzberg’s five parts and configurations without treating one structure as universally best.
takeaway: A structure connects work, coordination and authority; its suitability depends on the setting.

references.title: Mintzberg: Structure in 5’s (1980)

visuals.title: Five configurations: keep mechanism and component separate
visuals.note: A clarified comparison of the supplied table using Mintzberg’s original account for the professional-bureaucracy correction. These are ideal configurations, not a ranking or a universal organizational prescription.

ranges.heading: Parts and coordination mechanisms
ranges.introduction: The source illustrates the operating core, strategic apex, middle line, technostructure and support staff through school-system examples. Coordination and decentralization describe different dimensions; preserve that distinction.

ranges.heading: Five configurations and a corrected cell

paragraphs: The professional-bureaucracy row repeats “standardisation of skills” in the organizational-part column. Skills standardization is the coordinating mechanism; Mintzberg’s account emphasizes professionals in the operating core. The other configurations combine different mechanisms, parts and decision arrangements. The organization-as-system heading has no separate prose; its accompanying structure/culture/power diagram is retained as a related perspective, with unclear source labels disclosed.

references.title: Mintzberg: Structure in 5’s (1980)

title: Corporate parenting: how a centre adds or destroys value
summary: Compare restructuring, portfolio management, synergies and parental capabilities across business units.
takeaway: Owning several units is not itself an advantage: the centre must add more value than it costs or disrupts.

ranges.heading: Four approaches to the corporate parent
ranges.introduction: The notes distinguish a restructurer, portfolio manager, synergy manager and parental developer. Corporate-office size and intervention direction are descriptions of these models, not necessary conditions for success. “2+2=5” is a synergy metaphor, not a financial identity.

ranges.heading: What value-adding activity looks like
ranges.introduction: Review strategic intent, central services/resources, business-level challenge and coaching, expertise/knowledge sharing, and external linkages. Compare benefits with coordination costs and lost unit autonomy.

title: Business-model renewal: balance current performance and exploration
summary: Follow incremental renewal, transformative change and exploration through a delayed feedback model.
takeaway: Short-term performance gains can strengthen the current model while crowding out the search for a future one.

ranges.heading: Renewal, exploration and an unexplained buffer
ranges.introduction: The source lists three approaches, then places a “Buffer” heading beside a feedback diagram. The diagram supplies relationships that the prose does not explain; retain its signs and delay as a conceptual hypothesis, not measured causal coefficients. What the buffer contains or how it is funded is unspecified.

title: Business ethics: compare the reasons for a decision
summary: Use consequences, duties, rights, virtues and dialogue to examine decisions affecting other people.
takeaway: An ethical lens makes its reasons explicit; legal compliance alone does not resolve every responsibility.

visuals.title: Questions from different ethical lenses
rows: Who gains, who is harmed, and how uncertain are the outcomes?
Which obligations, rights and fair procedures constrain the action?
What character and relationships does the action express or damage?
Whose voice is missing, and can the reasons be justified to affected people?
visuals.note: A practical reading aid; it does not reduce each philosophical tradition to a complete one-sentence definition.

paragraphs: The supplied definitions concern right and wrong in business decisions, what organizations ought to do, and how policy and conduct reveal their stance. Compliance sets obligations, but a definition of ethics solely as exceeding the minimum is too narrow: respecting existing duties is also ethically significant. The quotations are retained with the source’s abbreviated attributions; complete editions/page references are not supplied.

ranges.heading: A map of ethical perspectives
ranges.introduction: Consequentialist approaches consider outcomes; duty, rights and justice approaches raise constraints and claims; virtue, care/feminist, discourse and postmodern approaches ask additional questions about character, relationships, dialogue and context. These are diverse traditions, not interchangeable formulas.

ranges.heading: Can ethics be learned, and why do these issues arise?

paragraphs: The claim that ethics cannot be taught is a view to examine, not an established educational result. “Leave ethics to government” is an incomplete description of Friedman. Privacy, working conditions, technology, environment and cross-border conduct create practical responsibilities. Volkswagen and Cambridge Analytica are historical cases with dated records, not grounds for a blanket claim about every present activity of the companies. The News Corporation example lacks a specific case/date in the notes and remains an incomplete historical prompt.

references.title: Friedman archive: business and profit
US DOJ: Volkswagen plea agreement, January 2017
FTC: Cambridge Analytica proceedings and orders, 2019

title: Business purpose: shareholders, stakeholders and governance
summary: Compare ownership, organizational purpose, accountability and claims about business performance.
takeaway: Serving capital providers and taking responsibility for affected people need not be treated as opposites.

visuals.title: Keep the dimensions separate
rows: Which interests is the organization trying to serve, and why?
Who holds which rights under the actual governance framework?
Who can inspect, challenge, remedy or constrain a decision?
Who is affected even when they lack votes or market power?
Which outcome, period and comparison supports the claim?
visuals.note: This separates questions that the source’s two-column contrasts sometimes combine.

ranges.heading: Business purpose and a misattributed stakeholder reference

paragraphs: The source gives business/management definitions and labels owner wealth as primary and other responsibilities as secondary. That is a normative framing, not a universal legal ordering. Friedman’s famous essay is dated 1970; the source’s 1962 reference needs a specific edition/text before assigning the quotation. Its “Evan and Friedman, 1988” appears to conflate William Evan and R. Edward Freeman. Freeman’s bibliography confirms collaboration, but the exact quoted sentence and page remain unverified. Both theories need fuller accounts than profit versus responsibility.

references.title: Darden: stakeholder theory
Freeman: bibliography and work with William Evan
Friedman archive: business and profit

ranges.heading: Compare governance arguments without promising returns

paragraphs: The table contrasts purpose, success measures, agency/conflict problems, director/stakeholder representation, management of stakeholders and social responsibility. Its claimed advantages/disadvantages—higher returns, less risk, stronger innovation or diluted monitoring—are unverified generalizations, not outcomes established for each model. Use the clarified comparison below; the full source table wording remains accessible.

references.title: Darden: stakeholder theory
Friedman archive: business and profit

paragraphs: Ownership, decision authority, legal duties and moral obligations are distinct. Stakeholder theory does not simply redefine a company as a legal joint venture, and shareholder approaches do not remove every duty to others. Whether cooperation improves an outcome depends on institutions, incentives and the decision. Retain these statements as propositions to examine rather than universally established descriptions.

references.title: Darden: stakeholder theory

title: Corporate social responsibility: commitments, stances and trade-offs
summary: Connect responsibilities to governance, conduct and the economic, social and environmental effects of a business.
takeaway: A model of responsibilities helps ask questions; it does not prove that a company fulfils them.

references.title: Archie Carroll: taking another look at the CSR pyramid (2016)

ranges.heading: What responsibility covers
ranges.introduction: The source definition and activity list cover workforce/community wellbeing, environment, philanthropy, social causes and employment standards. CSR is broader than donations; identify the business impacts and whose responsibilities are involved.

ranges.heading: Four stances: a teaching comparison
ranges.introduction: The source compares rationale, leadership, management, mode and relationships across four idealized stances. These are teaching categories, not a maturity score that every organization must maximize.

ranges.heading: Triple bottom line and the responsibility pyramid
ranges.introduction: Economic, social and environmental perspectives describe different effects, not a formula to add incomparable units. Carroll’s pyramid is contained in the accompanying image; its four layers and captions are retained in the visual and accessible comparison.

title: Responsible business practice: people, products, suppliers and power
summary: Turn ethical responsibilities into decisions about work, markets, supply chains, privacy and corporate conduct.
takeaway: Describe a specific practice and its evidence; a company name or a compliance claim is not a complete ethical assessment.

ranges.heading: Named examples need a dated case

paragraphs: The source mixes value-chain bargaining, labour conditions, fracking, alleged bribery, competition and corporate failures. These are different questions, with different evidence and legal outcomes. Its blanket statements about Primark/Nike, supermarkets and fracking are not verified as universal or current claims. Microsoft, British Airways, BHS and RBS need case-specific records before drawing conclusions. The linked case guide identifies the particular official findings verified for this collection; all original examples remain below.

references.title: CFTC: Barclays benchmark order, June 2012
US DOJ: BAE Systems guilty plea, March 2010

ranges.heading: Internal and external responsibilities
ranges.introduction: Use employee welfare, conditions and job design alongside environmental, product, marketing, supplier, employment, community and human-rights questions. Intellectual-property ownership depends on law and agreements; the notes’ blanket ownership statement is not a general legal rule. Fairness/positive-action examples require jurisdiction-specific context. “Energy conversation” appears intended as conservation; the original wording is preserved.

title: Make an ethical business decision: question, document and escalate
summary: Use legal, values, conscience and public-accountability questions while seeking informed review when the answer is unclear.
takeaway: A personal comfort test does not replace evidence, affected people’s rights or an appropriate escalation route.

visuals.title: A decision and escalation sequence
rows: Establish facts, uncertainty and affected people
Identify law, duties, rights and relevant policy
Compare harms, benefits, alternatives and conflicts
Seek an appropriate independent review or escalation
Record the reasons, decision, owner and follow-up
visuals.note: The short source checklist remains accessible. When a policy or lawful process requires stopping, a favourable personal impression is not an override.

ranges.heading: A short checklist attributed to Texas Instruments

paragraphs: The supplied checklist asks about law, values, conscience, public exposure and persistent questioning. Its attribution is retained as a historical source claim, not authenticated as the complete current TI code. TI’s official document sets out a broader set of principles, including responsible practices, privacy, conflicts, respect and use of resources. The newspaper test is a prompt for accountability, not a rule that publicity or embarrassment alone decides what is right.

references.title: Texas Instruments: Living our values and code of conduct

title: Business ethics cases: distinguish findings from shorthand
summary: Read selected historical official records with the date, actor and procedural outcome attached.
takeaway: Do not turn a settlement, guilty plea, allegation or undated example into a broader claim than the record supports.

references.title: US DOJ: Volkswagen plea agreement, January 2017
FTC: Cambridge Analytica proceedings and orders, 2019
CFTC: Barclays benchmark order, June 2012
US DOJ: BAE Systems guilty plea, March 2010

editorialSections.heading: Volkswagen: an announced plea agreement, 2017
paragraphs: On 11 January 2017 the US Department of Justice announced Volkswagen’s agreement to plead guilty over an emissions-testing scheme, with proposed criminal and civil penalties. This page cites that procedural stage and its date; it is not a complete account of every proceeding or a statement about all current vehicles.

editorialSections.heading: Cambridge Analytica: FTC proceedings, 2019
paragraphs: The FTC case record includes its action concerning deceptive representations connected to Facebook-user data and related settlements/orders. Read the particular respondent and document rather than treating every allegation or settlement in related Facebook proceedings as the same finding.

editorialSections.heading: Barclays: benchmark submissions, 2012
paragraphs: The CFTC’s 27 June 2012 order imposed a US$200 million penalty concerning attempted manipulation and false reporting of LIBOR/Euribor submissions. This is a specified regulatory action, not a statement that every transaction by the bank was improper.

editorialSections.heading: BAE Systems: the particular guilty plea, 2010
paragraphs: The US DOJ reported a 1 March 2010 guilty plea and US$400 million criminal fine concerning false statements and related US regulatory obligations. Do not replace this with an unqualified claim that it proved every bribery allegation associated with every country or contract.

editorialSections.heading: Other source examples: evidence still required
paragraphs: News Corporation, Primark, Nike, Microsoft, British Airways, BHS and RBS appear in abbreviated source examples. No specific finding is assigned here without the actual dated record. The original examples are retained in the relevant source disclosures, alongside the distinction between allegations, findings and ethical judgments.

ranges.heading: Mission, vision and values: sample statements
ranges.introduction: The source gives a mission example without a company attribution, a five-year vision example and a values statement. Treat these as supplied illustrations, not verified current corporate commitments.

ranges.heading: Purpose and identity prompts
ranges.introduction: Distinguish mission, vision, values, objectives, purpose, image and philosophy; decide which genuinely guides a choice.

ranges.heading: COVENANT and SMART: define useful outcomes
ranges.introduction: COVENANT is a source-specific mnemonic without attribution. SMART is a planning aid, not proof that a goal is worthwhile.

ranges.heading: Key results: useful qualities
ranges.introduction: Meaningful, measurable and memorable are qualities to discuss; a memorable number is not necessarily a valid outcome measure.

ranges.heading: Understand the pain without exploiting it
ranges.introduction: Investigate problem size, economic effects, alternatives, stress, beliefs and goals. Do not infer that fear-based persuasion is justified merely because a problem is painful.

ranges.heading: Operating changes to consider
ranges.introduction: Automation, delegation, relocation and digitalization are options to evaluate against the work and its constraints, not automatic improvements.

paragraphs: The random/informal/formal/dynamic ladder is an informal classification, not a named CMMI level system. Streamline and flexibility “indexes” are labels without formulas. The self-organization list names components, interactions, energy, feedback and emergence; it does not by itself establish an engineering specification.

ranges.heading: Review the operating location and procedures
ranges.introduction: Connect facilities/layout, purchasing, inventory, quality/customer service, labour, transport, taxes and regulation to the actual operation.

paragraphs: Standardized discretion, order and facility/design codes describe a systemization preference, not universal operating excellence. Company A–F grading lacks a rubric and cannot be used as a score. Optimization and improvement are headings without supplied methods.

ranges.heading: Economic value and operating-cost prompts
ranges.introduction: Distinguish opportunity and sunk costs, depreciation and allocation. Profitability rankings need a defined contribution/cost basis; eliminating a low-margin product can affect shared costs and the portfolio.

ranges.heading: Sourcing and operating arrangements
ranges.introduction: Outsourcing, subcontracting, offshoring, partnership and overhaul have different control/capability implications. The “replace” entry is explicitly a placeholder; no missing implementation guidance is invented.

ranges.heading: SCOR terms in this source
ranges.introduction: Source, Make, Deliver, Plan and Return identify a supplied version of the reference model. This is not represented as the complete current SCOR standard; map the actual supply chain and consult the applicable edition.

ranges.heading: Structures, information and a transition point

paragraphs: SCARF refers to Status, Certainty, Autonomy, Relatedness and Fairness; the source’s phrasing is abbreviated and does not validate a diagnostic score. The platform examples, information asymmetry, fragmentation, regulation and failure-cost prompts are hypotheses about industry structure, not proof that disruption is desirable. Distinguish innovation/geography/product-line growth from organizational design; lean and agility address different capabilities.

The notes list Courtship through Bureaucracy but do not supply a complete original model or diagnosis. Preserve these stages as the supplied excerpt, not a mandatory or complete lifecycle for every company.

title: Human development: Erikson’s eight-stage study outline
summary: Read the supplied trust, autonomy, identity and later-life themes as a psychological framework with context.
takeaway: These are human-development themes, not a corporate lifecycle, a diagnostic test or a timetable every person must follow.

ranges.heading: Eight psychosocial themes and associated strengths
ranges.introduction: The source lists age-period labels, tensions and virtues. People’s development and cultures vary; the outline is not a validated assessment of a particular reader or a substitute for an individual psychological evaluation.

ranges.heading: Visible artifacts, espoused beliefs and assumptions
ranges.introduction: Use these layers as questions about shared meanings; do not infer someone’s unconscious beliefs solely from uniforms or branding.

ranges.heading: People, authority and organizational capacity
ranges.introduction: Assess personnel, location, structure, philosophy and ownership alongside interaction, delegation, skill and motivation. Business continuity, disaster recovery and high availability are related but different requirements; plan them for the actual service and risk.

paragraphs: Analysis, design, development, implementation and evaluation describe a design cycle often used in learning contexts. The source provides the sequence only; it does not establish an automatic learning result.

ranges.heading: Development planning, learning and stopping
ranges.introduction: DICEE, leapfrogging and WAG/SWAG are source prompts. “Scientific” in SWAG does not make a guess a tested estimate. DFM and DFA ask different production questions; roadmaps, standards and polish should support the learning or delivery objective.

ranges.heading: Disruption and coordinated change
ranges.introduction: The five Ds and change-leadership actions are prompts, not evidence that disruption is inherently beneficial. Connect strategic intent, collaboration, communication and organization-wide learning to the change needed.

title: Operating process types: volume, variety, flow and constraints
summary: Compare manufacturing and service arrangements, then connect inventory, flow and throughput.
takeaway: A process label does not specify capacity; measure the actual system boundary, average flow and constraint.

references.title: MIT: Lean Thinking and Little’s Law

ranges.heading: Manufacturing process options
ranges.introduction: The notes associate project/job-shop/batch/line/continuous work with different volume patterns. These are typical teaching distinctions, not a rule that every continuous operation is fully automated.

paragraphs: For a stable flow system with consistent averages and boundary, Little’s relationship can be written average WIP = average throughput rate × average flow time. Rearranging gives flow time = WIP / throughput rate when the rate is positive. Units must agree: items divided by items/hour gives hours. Rated capacity is not automatically achieved throughput, so the source’s “capacity” parenthesis is unsafe as a substitution. Manage the constraint rather than optimizing every activity independently.

ranges.heading: Service process options
ranges.introduction: Professional service, service shop and mass service compare customization/variety and volume. They are idealized patterns; actual offerings can combine them.

ranges.heading: Project delivery and change responsibilities
ranges.introduction: The source links strategy, organization, motivation, teamwork, improvement and measurement. Clarify the actual project outcomes and ownership instead of assuming one project manager supplies all these functions.

paragraphs: Waterfall, Agile, Scrum and Kanban are not four interchangeable methodologies. Scrum is an Agile framework; Kanban can manage flow in Agile and other settings. The source’s labels are a compact reminder rather than complete definitions.

ranges.heading: A stage-and-gate sequence
ranges.introduction: The source alternates development stages with review/assessment gates. Gate labels do not alone specify acceptance criteria or a mandatory lifecycle for every project.

ranges.heading: Delivery measures and management prompts
ranges.introduction: The coordination-indicator label is undefined. Review timeliness, specification, staffing, deviations, earned value and key-person availability with baselines and ownership. More information is not automatically less intelligence: relevance, quality and decision context matter. A full-time project manager and master document are context-dependent recommendations.

ranges.heading: Leadership qualities in delivery
ranges.introduction: Responsive, responsible, systematic and adaptive describe different behaviours; translate them into observable project responsibilities.

ranges.heading: Fast tracking and crashing
ranges.introduction: These are different schedule-compression options with potential dependencies, costs and risks; evaluate the actual critical path and constraints.

ranges.heading: RACI as a responsibility prompt
ranges.introduction: Define Responsible, Accountable, Consulted and Informed for actual decisions or deliverables; a four-letter heading is not a complete assignment of authority.

ranges.heading: Solve-it prompts and shared ownership
ranges.introduction: Inviting contributions, persistence and connections can support a results-oriented culture. Persistence should remain open to evidence that a direction should change.

ranges.heading: Insurance categories to discuss
ranges.introduction: Workers’ compensation, liability, property/casualty, interruption, key-person, life/disability and payment-protection cover different exposures and insured parties. Names do not establish coverage, legal requirements or suitable policy terms.

ranges.heading: A broad risk identification menu
ranges.introduction: Keep competitive, economic, operational, legal/compliance, strategic, reputational, programme/project, innovation, country, quality, exchange, credit, interest, tax, resource/process, political, seasonal and counterparty exposures distinct where that improves decisions.

paragraphs: Mitigate, transfer, avoid, share and the source’s “retrain” are response labels; the latter appears intended as retain/accept, but the original is preserved. Transfer does not eliminate every residual responsibility. Delphi uses structured expert elicitation, often anonymously across rounds; it is not a guarantee of accurate prediction.

ranges.heading: Financial analyses to connect
ranges.introduction: Cash-flow, break-even and working-capital analysis answer different questions. Use the established definitions and formula references rather than inferring calculations from these three bare names.

ranges.heading: Strategic choices need market evidence
ranges.introduction: SWOT, the competitive landscape and market analysis are prompts to investigate. “Aggressive” strategy is not automatically suitable; identify evidence before relying on an unproven market.

paragraphs: Define the relevant customer and market forces before choosing a geography. SMSA/PMSA/CMSA are historical US statistical-area labels in these notes; do not treat this mixed list as the current official classification or apply it as a universal country system.

ranges.heading: Segmentation and practical reach
ranges.introduction: The geographic, demographic, psychographic and behavioural dimensions should support segments that can be measured, reached and served at a meaningful scale.

ranges.heading: Industry analysis and strategic opportunity
ranges.introduction: Describe suppliers, customers, distributors, competition, past performance and outlook before drawing an opportunity conclusion.

ranges.heading: Industry characteristics to investigate
ranges.introduction: Size, growth, capacity, profits, barriers, technology, innovation, capital, integration and scale need an actual industry, time period and evidence.

ranges.heading: RFM as a customer-analysis label
ranges.introduction: Recency, frequency and monetary value require defined events, a time window and a unit of analysis. The source supplies no scoring thresholds.

ranges.heading: Performance measures: correct the EBITDA expansion

paragraphs: Revenue, burn, headcount, historical performance and forecasts are different measures. The source expands earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortisation but abbreviates it “EBITA”; that expansion corresponds to EBITDA. EBITA normally excludes amortisation but not depreciation. Neither is cash flow, and no missing calculation is supplied.

The source expands SCAMPER as substitute, combine, adopt, modify, put to other use, eliminate and reverse. Versions use adapt rather than adopt; preserve the supplied version as a creative prompt, not an evidence test.

ranges.heading: CMMI, Six Sigma and TQM are different approaches

paragraphs: These three names are supplied without further detail. Capability maturity, variation/process improvement and organization-wide quality management address different concerns; cross-link the existing readings instead of treating the labels as one methodology.

Embryonic/growth/maturity/ageing and the strategy/execution/talent slogan are brief source labels. F3EA is a military-origin find/fix/finish/exploit/analyse sequence; it is not a generic endorsed business operating procedure. No missing method or attribution is fabricated.

references.title: US Army: F3EA in a military targeting context (2024)

ranges.heading: Two military-strategy references
ranges.introduction: Sun Tzu and Clausewitz are bare names here, not an additional historical text. Use the existing historical reading and distinguish modern business reflection from original material.

ranges.heading: Business-model patterns and a different DISC acronym

paragraphs: Here DISC means Define, Identify, Segmentise/Sort, Classify; it must not be merged with DISC personality models. Matchmaker, pay-in-advance, subscription, scarcity-based and service-to-product are model patterns illustrated with supplied company examples, not verified current classifications. “Recession-proof” is an unsupported resilience claim. Lifecycle stages also need a defined object: a product, business or industry need not follow the same path.

ranges.heading: Resources, activities and offerings
ranges.introduction: The source connects resource base, activity system/value chain and product offering/value proposition with markets. This is a useful complement to a canvas; the diagram’s two-way relationships are preserved rather than reducing it to a one-way value chain.

ranges.heading: International strategy: purpose, choice and orientation
ranges.introduction: The source links market size, investment scale, learning and location with whether/what/where/how questions and ethnocentric/polycentric/regiocentric/geocentric orientations. Rapid expansion in response to weak patent protection is an argument requiring context, not a universal recommendation.

paragraphs: The Glyn and Sutcliffe quotation is dated 1992 in the notes. It concerns the authors’ historical comparison; no complete publication/page is supplied. Preserve it as a dated research prompt rather than current evidence of globalization’s level.

ranges.heading: Stakeholder groups and mapping questions
ranges.introduction: The source names owners, finance, activists, customers, managers, unions, employees, associations, competitors, suppliers, government and political groups. Map influence and interest to plan engagement; the matrix does not decide whose interests ethically matter.

ranges.heading: Power and interest: a map, not a moral ranking

paragraphs: The diagram assigns minimal effort, keep informed, keep satisfied and key players to four influence/interest quadrants. These are engagement heuristics; low power does not remove rights or the need to prevent harm.
